questions.text: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
questions.solution:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond.

[latex]\text{SMTP}[/latex] (mail), [latex]\text{FTP}[/latex] (file transfer), and [latex]\text{HTTP}[/latex] (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast.

Answer: DHCP

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to the interaction of a web browser with a web server using HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex]?
questions.solution:
HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and pipelining over a single TCP connection:

- True: Multiple objects of the same webpage, if hosted on the same server, can be fetched over one persistent TCP connection — this is exactly the point of persistent connections.
- False: A single TCP connection is between one client and one specific server; objects stored on a different server require a separate TCP connection to that server. So this statement is false.
- True: HTTP/1.1 supports pipelining — a client can send a new request before the response to a previous request has been fully received, over the same connection.
- True: Since the TCP connection persists (is not closed after one request/response), multiple different webpages/resources from the same server can be downloaded over that same single connection, one after another.

Answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true (same-server multi-object download, pipelining, multiple pages over one connection); statement about different servers over the same connection is false.

Click here for detail solution
options: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, if the objects are stored in the same server
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, even if they are stored in different servers
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates sending a request for downloading one object without waiting for a previously requested object to be downloaded completely
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple webpages on the same server to be downloaded over a single TCP connection

questions.text:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.

(i) HTTP GET request for the index page
(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address
(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object
(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server

Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer ?
questions.solution:
Order in which the packets leave the computer:
1. (ii) DNS request [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the IP address of the server is needed before anything else (caches are empty).
2. (iv) TCP SYN [latex]\text{---}[/latex] open the TCP connection with the server.
3. (i) GET index page [latex]\text{---}[/latex] first request on the connection.
4. (iii) GET image [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the browser knows about the image only after it receives and parses the index page.

Answer: (ii), (iv), (i), (iii)

questions.text:
Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host) over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached anywhere across all DNS servers.
Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers in the DNS hierarchy. The round trip time between the local host and the web server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML file associated with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on the same web server.
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?
questions.solution:
DNS (iterative, 3 tiers: root, TLD, authoritative) = 3 RTT.

Non-persistent, 5 parallel connections: base HTML = TCP setup + request = 2 RTT. The 10 objects go in 2 batches of 5, each batch 2 RTT (new connection each) = 4 RTT.
Total = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 RTT.

Persistent with pipelining: TCP setup 1 RTT + HTML 1 RTT + all 10 objects pipelined in 1 RTT.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 RTT.

Answer: 9 RTTs (non-persistent, 5 parallel) and 6 RTTs (persistent with pipelining)

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: 7 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
5 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.

questions.text: Consider the resolution of the domain name [latex]www.gate.org.in[/latex] by a DNS resolver. Assume that no resource records are cached anywhere across the DNS servers and that iterative query mechanism is used in the resolution. The number of DNS query-response pairs involved in completely resolving the domain name is .
questions.solution:
With iterative resolution and empty caches, the resolver asks each level in turn:
1. Root server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to the .in server
2. .in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to org.in
3. org.in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] refers to gate.org.in
4. gate.org.in server [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns the IP of www.gate.org.in

Answer: 4
